newsitem.title: USA: Leaders hold second day of Mideast summit talks.
newsitem.headline: Leaders hold second day of Mideast summit talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton sought on Wednesday to persuade the leaders of Israel and the Palestinians to translate their new civility into concrete steps to reinvigorate the Middle East peace process.

But there apparently were no guarantees of tangible results at the emergency summit that on Tuesday saw Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat meet alone with aides for three hours.

It was only the second face-to-face meeting between the two leaders, who previously have displayed barely disguised disdain for each other. The crisis summit was called after bloody clashes between Palestinians and Israelis last week that threatened to scuttle the whole peace process.

An Israeli official said Netanyahu wanted another private meeting with Arafat "to iron out differences" before going to the White House on Wednesday, but a Palestinian spokesman could not immediately confirm it would be held.
Working level meetings went on through the night and Secretary of State Warren Christopher conferred with top aides of Netanyahu and Arafat in his office on Wednesday morning.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry was non-commital on the progress so far. "We are neither encouraged nor discouraged. We are determined to help the parties," he told reporters.
Another U.S. official who declined to be identified, asked by Reuters if there was any substantive progress to point to, said: "The meetings themselves. The fact that the talks are continuing."
He added: "We are going to continue to stay out of a discussion of the substance until that is appropriate, and we're not there yet."
Gun battles and clashes in the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week took the lives of 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
Clinton was scheduled to join Netanyahu, Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein in the White House Blue Room for a meeting set tentatively for 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT).
If the day unfolded as the White House expected, the group session was to be followed by a working lunch.

The leaders would then make public statements summarizing their two days of talks at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) -- a sign that they expected to have something to announce -- but few White House insiders expected the news conference to start at anything close to the scheduled time.

On the only concrete point divulged by officials about Tuesday's talks, Israel said it stood firm against U.S. pressure to set a date to complete a long-delayed pullback of troops from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Palestinians view Hebron, the last and most sensitive of the cities slated for handover under an agreement sealed at the White House one year ago, as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he reluctantly inherited when he came to power at the head of a hardline government in June.

Last week's fighting was sparked by Israel's decision to open another entrance to a tourist tunnel alongside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, holy to Moslems and Jews. But it also reflected Arab frustrations at what they consider Israel's slow pace in pursuing peace accords.

Palestinians demand that Israel close the tunnel, carry out the pullback from Hebron -- home to 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews -- and ease a closure barring Palestinians from jobs in Gaza and the West Bank.

Netanyahu has toughened his stance since the violence erupted, accusing Arafat of ordering his police force to fire at Israelis guns the peace deal provided. But a new opinion poll on Tuesday showed 80 percent of Israelis want him to press ahead with peace moves.
